ideas.title: The Unicorn Upgrade Is a Whale Tooth
ideas.premise: What if today Rex's premium unicorn-powered leadership accessory turned out to be a narwhal tooth, echoing the material identification of a 1615 sceptre?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Unicorn Upgrade Is a Whale Tooth history

rationale.curiosity: A specific object behind a mythical sales story gives the reveal an evidence-based reversal.
rationale.cast_comedy: Mia can resolve Rex's fictional branding confusion while Pip waits for the promised leadership improvement.
rationale.modern_contrast: Luxury product claims contrast with a cataloged historical symbol of authority.
rationale.primary_sources: The Vienna Treasury identifies WS XIa 2, maker, date and actual narwhal material; original early records need separate consultation.

cast_gags.crow: Raven distinguishes a historical unicorn belief from the actual animal material.
cast_gags.pip: Pip waits for Rex's fictional accessory to improve an ordinary meeting.
cast_gags.mia: Mia presents the museum identification and a separate educational narwhal silhouette.
cast_gags.rex: Rex quietly turns his invented unicorn-certified label face down.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy brings the meeting agenda and asks whether the whale tooth can take minutes.

sources.institution: Treasury, Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: Sceptre; Andreas Osenbruck; 1615; Prague; inventory WS XIa 2; narwhal shaft identification
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The leadership product and certification are fiction. The museum distinguishes early unicorn claims from the actual narwhal material. Mythological powers are not real effects; no medical use, antidote claim or suggestion to acquire animal material is offered. The early documentary wording is mediated through a modern catalog, not directly inspected.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Consult the cited early records and material analysis before naming who believed the claim, assigning a purchase value or attributing a specific documented political intention.

ideas.title: Your Expense Report Is a Bundle of Knots
ideas.era: Andes; object catalog date AD 1425-1532; attributed probably Inka
ideas.premise: What if today Pip submitted the numerical part of his expense report as knotted cords instead of a spreadsheet, inspired by an Inka khipu?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Expense Report Is a Bundle of Knots history

rationale.curiosity: A physical report reveals a real record-keeping technology with a concrete everyday contrast.
rationale.cast_comedy: Pip can deliver a carefully organized report while Rex mistakes unfamiliar storage for missing information.
rationale.modern_contrast: A fictional expense workflow makes numerical recording legible without treating the historical system as primitive.
rationale.primary_sources: Smithsonian NMAI identifies object 14/3866 with an attributed culture and date range; its individual message has not been decoded here.

cast_gags.crow: Raven introduces a sophisticated numerical record, not a joke about an allegedly illiterate people.
cast_gags.pip: Pip brings a clearly fictional cord report to the expense meeting.
cast_gags.mia: Mia points out that Rex's failure to understand a format does not make its information disappear.
cast_gags.rex: Rex asks where the imaginary export-to-spreadsheet button is.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy lays out a large modern teaching key for the fictional prop without touching any original object.

sources.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: Inka khipu; catalog 14/3866; probably Inka (attributed); AD 1425-1532; Chulpaca, Ica, Peru
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The modern expense report and teaching key are fiction. The object record describes quantitative uses in general, not a decoded expense ledger for this specimen. Preserve the attribution probably Inka. Do not claim all khipus are fully read, all meanings are purely numeric, or Andean people lacked complex communication.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Obtain a specialist reading and the accession documentation before assigning any exact value, category, owner or administrative purpose to these particular cords.

ideas.title: The Meeting Clock Has a Peacock
ideas.era: England and Saint Petersburg; automaton cataloged 1770s; arrival described in 1781
ideas.premise: What if today Rex replaced the meeting timer with a monumental mechanical peacock, owl and cockerel, inspired by the Hermitage Peacock Clock?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Meeting Clock Has a Peacock history

rationale.curiosity: A simple timekeeping request revealing an entire mechanical display gives the hook a clear physical escalation.
rationale.cast_comedy: The cast can expose Rex's preference for prestige over usefulness while respecting the actual craftsmanship.
rationale.modern_contrast: A modern meeting timer contrasts with a documented courtly automaton.
rationale.primary_sources: Hermitage identifies Cox's clock and contextualizes its assembly and transport; claims about surviving uniqueness require independent comparison.

cast_gags.crow: Raven watches the decorative birds as objects, without gaining accessories or changing his identity.
cast_gags.pip: Pip requests a five-minute timer and receives an imaginary ceremonial unveiling.
cast_gags.mia: Mia searches for the documented clock dial while Rex admires the display.
cast_gags.rex: Rex postpones the fictional meeting to explain how efficient the new timer will be.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy holds a paper agenda and points out that the explanation has already used the meeting time.

sources.institution: The State Hermitage Museum via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: The Peacock Clock; James Cox; Date Created 1770s; explanatory passage on cockerel, owl, dial and 1781 arrival
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The meeting timer and office delivery are fiction. The object is a ceremonial mechanical display, not an ordinary household alarm. research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Inspect a technical record before assigning exact animation order, timing, power source, conservation state or original component history.

ideas.title: Your Home Cinema Has Thirty Lines
ideas.era: Europe, circa 1930; Baird Televisor described by the Cinematheque francaise
ideas.premise: What if today Rex sold Pip a home-cinema upgrade whose picture had only thirty vertical lines, like the mechanical Baird Televisor described by a film museum?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Home Cinema Has Thirty Lines history

rationale.curiosity: The mismatch between a grand sales promise and a tiny limited image provides a measurable historical reveal.
rationale.cast_comedy: Pip's attempt to watch and Rex's fictional marketing claims can escalate while Mia identifies what the mechanism actually did.
rationale.modern_contrast: Modern display expectations make early mechanical scanning easy to contrast without belittling the engineering.
rationale.primary_sources: The film museum provides a detailed institutional account; a standalone object accession and contemporary manual still need inspection.

cast_gags.crow: Raven distinguishes an important engineering experiment from Rex's imaginary modern sales pitch.
cast_gags.pip: Pip leans toward a harmless editorial reconstruction of the small display.
cast_gags.mia: Mia labels the thirty-line reconstruction and explains it is not authentic surviving programme footage.
cast_gags.rex: Rex hands Pip an oversized fictional premium-cinema brochure.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy folds the brochure into a viewing frame and discovers that it cannot add image detail.

sources.institution: The Cinematheque francaise via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: John Logie Baird's Televisor; circa 1930 receiver explanation; thirty-vertical-line picture and revolving-disc sections
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The modern sales pitch is fiction and the source is institutional interpretation, not a directly inspected operating manual. Do not apply one receiver's specifications to every early television system, claim the first television ever, or present a reconstruction as original broadcast footage. No actual playback or rendering occurs in this scout.

ideas.title: The Teacup Has a Built-In Guard
ideas.premise: What if today your cafe added a built-in guard to a teacup to keep a moustache dry, as on an 1876 souvenir cup?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Teacup Has a Built-In Guard history

rationale.curiosity: A familiar cup with an unexpected protective feature makes the reveal immediately understandable.
rationale.cast_comedy: Rex can overcomplicate an ordinary design feature while Mia explains its actual purpose.
rationale.modern_contrast: An imaginary accessory launch contrasts with a specific nineteenth-century souvenir.
rationale.primary_sources: Smithsonian locates nmah_1065116 and explicitly states the moustache function; retrieval and manufacturing provenance remain separate checks.

cast_gags.crow: Raven introduces the documented function without changing anyone's canonical facial features.
cast_gags.pip: Pip presents an empty modern demonstration cup and asks what its extra ledge does.
cast_gags.mia: Mia explains the historical moustache guard using a separate paper diagram.
cast_gags.rex: Rex launches a fictional premium protection tier for an ordinary tea break.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy sets a miniature umbrella beside the prop cup and asks whether it has enough protection yet.

sources.institution: Smithsonian Institution / National Museum of American History
sources.locator: Centennial International Exhibition of 1876 Souvenir Moustache Cup; nmah_1065116; Larry Zim World's Fair Collection
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The cafe launch is fiction. A souvenir proves a particular object and its cataloged function, not that all men wore moustaches or that every cup had a guard. No moustache is added to the immutable cast, and no unverified fair attendance, product-first or invention claim is used. Failed retrieval leaves the source locally unverified.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Confirm the exact guard shape from an inspected object image and locate a maker mark or patent before identifying its inventor, price or manufacturing location.
